directAnswer: Pope John X (reigned 914–928) was a former archbishop of Ravenna who became one of the most politically active popes of the tenth century. He helped organize the Christian coalition that destroyed the Saracen stronghold on the Garigliano River in 915, crowned Berengar I emperor, and was ultimately deposed and imprisoned by the faction of Marozia, dying in captivity.

sections.h2: From Romagna to the See of Ravenna
paras: John came from Tossignano, near Imola in the Romagna. He served as a deacon at Bologna and was named archbishop of Ravenna, the most important see in northern Italy after Milan, around 905. That experience in a major metropolitan see gave him administrative and political skills that he would bring to Rome.

His transfer from Ravenna to Rome in 914 was unusual at the time, because moving a bishop from one see to another was still viewed with suspicion. The chronicler Liutprand of Cremona, writing decades later and hostile to the Roman nobility, claimed John owed his advancement to Theodora, wife of the powerful Theophylact. Modern historians treat that story with caution, but it is clear that John came to power with the support of the ruling Roman family.

For decades a band of Saracen raiders had held a fortified camp near the mouth of the Garigliano River, between Rome and Naples, from which they plundered the countryside and monasteries such as Monte Cassino. John X made its destruction a priority. He brought together an unusual alliance: Alberic I of Spoleto, the Lombard princes of Capua and Benevento, the coastal cities of Naples and Gaeta, and a Byzantine force.

In 915 the allied army besieged and overran the stronghold, and the pope was present in the field with the troops. The victory removed a threat that had hung over central Italy for a generation and gave the papacy a prestige it had lacked for years. Later that year John crowned Berengar I of Friuli as emperor in Rome.

sections.h2: Croatia, Ravenna and the Wider Church
paras: John's correspondence shows him engaged well beyond Rome. Around 925 he wrote to the Croatian ruler Tomislav and the clergy of Dalmatia about the church synod at Split, pressing for the use of Latin in the liturgy rather than Slavonic and supporting the authority of the archbishop of Split. He also intervened in Frankish church affairs, including the troubled succession to the see of Reims.

After the deaths of Theophylact and Alberic I, power in Rome passed to Marozia, Theophylact's daughter, and her husband Guy, margrave of Tuscany. John sought a counterweight by allying with Hugh of Provence, whom he met at Mantua in 926. The alliance alarmed Marozia's party. In 928 the pope's brother Peter was killed in the Lateran, and John himself was seized and imprisoned.

He died in confinement shortly afterward, probably in 928 or 929. Later writers said he was smothered, though the exact circumstances cannot be confirmed. His fall opened a period in which the papacy was closely controlled by Marozia's family.

keyFacts: Reigned c. March 914 to c. May 928
Born at Tossignano in the Romagna; previously archbishop of Ravenna
Helped lead the coalition that took the Saracen fortress on the Garigliano (915)
Deposed and imprisoned by Marozia's faction; died in captivity

faqs.question: Did Pope John X really fight in a battle?
faqs.answer: Contemporary and near-contemporary sources place him with the allied army at the Garigliano in 915. He accompanied the forces that besieged and destroyed the Saracen camp, which was unusual for a pope.

faqs.question: Why was Pope John X deposed?
faqs.answer: His alliance with Hugh of Provence threatened the power of Marozia and her husband Guy of Tuscany, who controlled Rome. They had him arrested in 928, and he died in prison.

faqs.question: What did John X decide about the Slavonic liturgy in Croatia?
faqs.answer: In letters connected with the synod of Split around 925, he urged the Croatian clergy to celebrate the liturgy in Latin and discouraged the spread of Slavonic worship.
